findings.source_passage: Before me stretched the portentous, menacing road of a new decade.
findings.source_locator: After 'I was thirty,' before the seven-o'clock departure for Long Island
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence completes one of the novel's most quoted micro-passages: 'I was thirty. Before me stretched the portentous, menacing road of a new decade.' The birthday reflection is a critically noted intrusion of Nick's voice; excising the second sentence strips the passage of its rhetorical weight and leaves only the bare fact.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence immediately after 'I was thirty.' in the draft: 'Before me stretched the portentous, menacing road of a new decade.'

findings.source_passage: her left breast was swinging loose like a flap, and there was no need to listen for the heart beneath. The mouth was wide open and ripped a little at the corners, as though she had choked a little in giving up the tremendous vitality she had stored so long.
findings.source_locator: Michaelis section, description of Myrtle's body after the accident
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is the novel's most viscerally distinctive piece of prose—critically noted for its brutal physicality and for the grotesque irony of 'vitality' attached to a corpse. The draft replaces it with 'there was no need to listen for the heart beneath,' losing the specific images that give the death its interpretive and stylistic signature.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the two graphic sentences verbatim: 'her left breast was swinging loose like a flap, and there was no need to listen for the heart beneath. The mouth was wide open and ripped a little at the corners, as though she had choked a little in giving up the tremendous vitality she had stored so long.'

findings.source_passage: Daisy and Jordan lay upon an enormous couch, like silver idols weighing down their own white dresses against the singing breeze of the fans.
findings.source_locator: First description of Daisy and Jordan in the Buchanan drawing-room
findings.why_it_matters: The full simile—'silver idols weighing down their own white dresses against the singing breeze of the fans'—is a visually iconic and critically remarked image of Daisy and Jordan as decorative, languid, and inhuman. The draft retains 'like silver idols' but drops the rest of the image, losing the stylistic and interpretive substance.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the simile to its full form: 'like silver idols weighing down their own white dresses against the singing breeze of the fans.'

findings.source_passage: There is no confusion like the confusion of a simple mind, and as we drove away Tom was feeling the hot whips of panic. His wife and his mistress, until an hour ago secure and inviolate, were slipping precipitately from his control.
findings.source_locator: Opening of the drive from Wilson's garage toward New York, after the valley-of-ashes stop
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is a key moment of narratorial commentary on Tom's psychology—stylistically distinctive and interpretively important for understanding Tom's double exposure. Its absence removes Nick's ironic distance and the parallel structure that the novel depends on for its moral architecture.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the passage immediately after Tom pulls away from Wilson's garage: 'There is no confusion like the confusion of a simple mind, and as we drove away Tom was feeling the hot whips of panic. His wife and his mistress, until an hour ago secure and inviolate, were slipping precipitately from his control.'

findings.source_passage: The prolonged and tumultuous argument that ended by herding us into that room eludes me, though I have a sharp physical memory that, in the course of it, my underwear kept climbing like a damp snake around my legs and intermittent beads of sweat raced cool across my back.
findings.source_locator: Plaza Hotel suite, opening of the room scene
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the novel's most distinctive voice-establishing asides—Nick's self-deprecating, physically precise register is signature Fitzgerald. The draft skips directly to the room, losing the comic-grotesque texture that marks this narrator's consciousness.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence about the underwear and sweat as the lead-in to the Plaza scene; it is short enough to include verbatim and essential to voice.

findings.source_passage: Gatsby's eyes followed it momentarily; he raised his hand and pointed across the bay. 'I'm right across from you.' … Slowly the white wings of the boat moved against the blue cool limit of the sky. Ahead lay the scalloped ocean and the abounding blessed isles.
findings.source_locator: Veranda scene after luncheon, before returning inside
findings.why_it_matters: The vision of the 'scalloped ocean and the abounding blessed isles' is a lyric moment of symbolic geography—the Edenic horizon Gatsby believes he is approaching—critically noted as a counterpoint to the ash-heaps. Its absence thins the symbolic texture of the chapter's middle.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert a brief version of the veranda exchange and the closing lyric: 'Ahead lay the scalloped ocean and the abounding blessed isles,' before moving to luncheon.

findings.source_passage: only the dead dream fought on as the afternoon slipped away, trying to touch what was no longer tangible, struggling unhappily, undespairingly, toward that lost voice across the room.
findings.source_locator: After Gatsby begins talking excitedly to Daisy following Tom's exposure of the drugstores
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reproduces this passage but removes the crucial framing sentence that precedes it: 'so he gave that up.' Without that pivot, the 'dead dream' clause loses the explicit surrender that makes it a dirge rather than mere description—a critical distinction for readings of Gatsby's delusion.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full framing: 'But with every word she was drawing further and further into herself, so he gave that up, and only the dead dream fought on…'

findings.source_passage: I picked it up with a weary bend and handed it back to her, holding it at arm's length and by the extreme tip of the corners to indicate that I had no designs upon it—but everyone near by, including the woman, suspected me just the same.
findings.source_locator: Train scene, the woman who drops her pocketbook in the heat
findings.why_it_matters: This brief comic-paranoid incident is a characteristic Nick aside that establishes the narrator's ironic self-awareness in the heat-oppressed opening. Its absence is minor but contributes to the flattening of the train sequence's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert one sentence summarizing the pocketbook incident and the comic suspicion that followed, to preserve the narrator's register.

summary: The draft has two high-severity signature losses—the 'portentous, menacing road of a new decade' sentence and the full physicality of Myrtle's death—plus four medium-severity losses of voice-establishing and interpretive passages (the 'simple mind' commentary, the Plaza underwear aside, the 'scalloped ocean' lyric, and the 'so he gave that up' pivot before the dead-dream passage), requiring regeneration.
